_note: Every gameplay number lives here. Nothing tunable should be a const in a .gd file any more. tools/sim.gd plays hundreds of days against this file and prints the curves, so a change here can be checked without playing.
_contract: THE BALANCE CONTRACT. tools/sim.gd measures these from SIMULATED play, and tests/run.gd asserts them. The previous version asserted hand-set state, which is how a grade model broken in four places passed 218 tests.
bare room, perfect teaching  -> ~0.63  a C
full room, never helped      -> ~0.71  a C
full room, perfect teaching  -> ~0.97  an A
Homework is a bonus on top, so a good term survives one bad lesson.

grade_bands._note: Where a numeric grade (0..1) lands as a letter. Used to hardcode as A>=0.88, B>=0.75, C>=0.62, D>=0.50, E>=0.38 -- the contract's own bare-room-perfect-teaching row (0.63) sat 1 point above the C floor, and realistic imperfect play (not perfect, just decent) landed BELOW it, in D. Softened so the same three contract scenarios keep their letters with real margin instead of a hair's width, and so trying-but-imperfect play actually reads as a C rather than a D. Below 'e' is an F.
grade_bands._contract_check: bare-room-perfect (0.63) and full-room-never-helped (0.71) must both stay C -- so 'c' must sit below both and 'b' must sit above both. full-room-perfect (0.97) must stay A.

lesson._note: work_seconds is how much UNSTUCK time a student needs to finish. lesson_seconds is the clock you are racing. A stalled student's timer freezes, so an unreached student simply never finishes — that is the whole pressure.
lesson._uncollected_note: Seconds a finished sheet may sit on a desk before the game says out loud, once per run, that it only counts when collected. Uncollected work HALVES that child's lesson grade at the bell (see grade.uncollected_penalty), and nothing said so. Not instant: the player may already be walking over, and a nudge that fires the moment a child finishes would be noise rather than teaching.

class._desk_note: A desk is a SEAT you bought, and the class grows into it. The cap was hard-wired at 8 from the beginning -- eight desks in a 20x11 room, and no way to have more. Buying one costs coins AND floor: a desk needs two free tiles with an aisle to the door, so a bigger room is what makes a bigger class possible rather than a number in a table.

homework._note: not_done_forgiveness: a student who misses homework is asked again the next night rather than being locked out forever.

room_upkeep._note: Daily clutter -- trash and spills, scripts/interact/mess.gd. Legwork with a flat coin tip, not a grade input: nothing here touches grade/room_base or anything the balance contract measures, so it is exempt from that contract on purpose.

term._note: A run is a term. On the last day the class sits an exam scored on everything you built up, and that is the score you are playing for.
term._exam_note: The exam is a child's own record, plus a little for the room you sat them in. It used to be average*0.75 + room*0.35, which counted the room TWICE -- room_score is already inside every daily grade -- and marked down everyone whose average was above 0.39. A child who averaged an A all term sat the exam in a bare room and got a B.
term._next_term_note: What survives a term. The ROOM you built, the curriculum you learned, your own level and perks, and your coins all carry over -- they are the things you spent the term making, and taking them away would make the term a sandbox rather than a chapter. What does NOT carry is the class: children who passed move up and out, and children who did not stay for another go, keeping their record.
term._target_note: How many children must pass for you to keep the job. It rises every term, and it is the only thing in the game you can LOSE to. Without it the room gets better every term against a difficulty that never moves, so by the third term nothing you do matters. The target is what makes a better room necessary rather than merely pleasant.

upkeep._note: Furniture needs replacing. A per-item daily cost means coins never just pile up, and a huge room you cannot afford is a real decision.

teacher._note: The teacher's own numbers. speed and pick_radius used to be consts in actor.gd/interactable.gd -- they were missed when everything else moved here, because they read as physics rather than balance. They live here now so perks can raise them and tools/sim.tscn can model a levelled teacher.

student._note: Students improve just by being taught. A level nudges aptitude and diligence a little; ready_level is when they can be sent up. XP STOPS at ready_level+hold_grace: a child kept long past readiness has learned what you can teach them, which is a soft cost for holding them back rather than a punishment.

concepts._note: What knowing your material is worth. It scales with how much of the lesson the child actually got through, so it rewards TEACHING rather than merely turning up: a class you never went near gains almost nothing from your expertise. Small per concept and capped, and worth zero on day one, which is what keeps the three-row contract unmoved.

room._note: Buying floor space. Priced per TILE of new floor and rising with each expansion, so a bigger room is a real investment rather than a thing you tick off on day two. The room only grows right and down: the door is a fixed point on the left wall and everything already placed must keep its coordinates.

test._note: The end-of-unit test. Playable only after you have taught the unit enough times to have unlocked its concepts. It is the one instrument you cannot intervene in: no helping, no collecting, no stalls. What it measures is the classroom you BUILT and the children you developed, not how well you ran round the room today -- which is exactly why it is worth more than a lesson.

quiz._note: The in-lesson diagnostic. Carries NO direct grade weight on purpose -- the three-row balance contract is measured without one, and a quiz that paid grade would quietly move the pillar. What it buys is information: who is behind, while there is still lesson left to do something about it. It costs 14 of a 45-second lesson, raised from 10 after the term simulator showed quizzing paying about ten times the coins at an identical grade -- which is not a decision, it is a formality.
quiz._buff_note: A quiz cost 14 of a 45-second lesson and returned 1.5s of work per student plus 6s per flagged child -- break-even at about four students on time alone, and nothing of it survived the bell. It now leaves the class FOCUSED for the rest of the lesson: they have just been made to think, so they get stuck less. That is the retrieval-practice claim the 1.5s was already gesturing at, made into something you can feel.

graduation._note: What sending a child up is worth. Scaled by readiness, so graduating someone the moment they qualify pays less than seeing them through.

coaching._note: Bought from a student's own file. Cost multiplies per purchase FOR THAT CHILD, so the decision is who to invest in rather than levelling everyone flat.

brisk_walk.name: Brisk Walk
brisk_walk.blurb: You get around the room faster.

long_reach.name: Long Reach
long_reach.blurb: Help from a little further away.

steady_hands.name: Steady Hands
steady_hands.blurb: Carry any amount of work at once.

calm_presence.name: Calm Presence
calm_presence.blurb: Students near you get stuck less often.

practised_marker.name: Practised Marker
practised_marker.blurb: Judge fewer sheets a night; the rest go at your usual standard.

perk_effects._note: Per RANK. brisk_walk adds to teacher.speed, long_reach to pick_radius, calm_presence multiplies the stall chance of students within its radius, practised_marker removes that many sheets from the nightly pile.

_items_note: 'teaches' means owning the item unlocks that concept outright -- which is what finally ties the furniture you buy to the curriculum. 'needs' gates an item behind a concept you must already know, so the shop grows as you teach rather than only as you earn.

traits._note: One per child, rolled at enrolment and never changed. Every trait has a real mechanical hook -- a trait that only shows up as a line of text on the class list is decoration, and decoration is what makes a player stop reading the list. 'blurb' is what the file says about them; the player is never told the numbers.

quiet.name: Quiet
quiet.blurb: Will not say when they are lost.

curious.name: Curious
curious.blurb: Asks about everything. Gets stuck more, learns more.

chatty.name: Chatty
chatty.blurb: Talks to whoever is sitting next to them.

copier.name: Copies

bright.name: Bright spark
bright.blurb: Finishes early and helps the next desk along.

loud.name: Loud
loud.blurb: Works well enough, but narrates everything they do.

shy.name: Shy

anchor.blurb: Solid and dependable, but keeps their head down.

ghost.name: Ghost
ghost.blurb: Flies under the radar by borrowing heavily.

disruption._note: Messing about, which is NOT the same as being stuck. A stuck child has stopped and wants you; a disruptive one has stopped and is stopping the children either side of them, and it spreads along the desks until somebody deals with it. Both sources are things the player caused: boredom is finished work you never came to collect, frustration is a child left stuck too long. Neither is bad luck.

voice._note: Raising your voice. The only verb in the game that is not attached to a landmark -- but it still depends on WHERE YOU ARE STANDING, because it only reaches desks within earshot. It settles the room; it does not teach anybody anything, so a stuck child still needs you at their desk. That is the line that keeps walking the room the game.

inspection._note: What an inspector actually judges. Three things, and you can prepare for all three, because the visit is announced the evening before -- an unannounced judgement is weather, not a decision. Each is something the game already tracks: the room you built, the lesson they watched, and whether you know the material you are teaching.

_flat_note: 'flat' means the item lies on the floor or hangs on the wall, so it gets no contact shadow -- a rug with a shadow under it looks like it is hovering.

teaching._note: Standing at the front and TEACHING. Work only advances while the class is paying attention, and attention only comes from you. Before this a lesson ran itself and the player's whole job was reacting to bubbles -- there was nothing to DO with the time between them.
teaching._decay_note: Attention DECAYS rather than switching off. As a hard on/off, a two second trip to help one child froze seven others dead, which reads as the game being broken rather than as a trade-off. Decay means a short trip costs a slice of progress and a long absence costs all of it.
teaching._drift_note: How far attention has to fall before the game says out loud, once per run, that work only moves while you are at the front. Deliberately NOT the moment you step away -- walking to a stuck child is the game, and a nudge fired then would read as 'do not do that'. It fires once the absence has actually cost something, which is when the sentence means anything.

difficulty._note: How much a lesson's difficulty rating actually moves. Difficulty 3 is the neutral middle: work_mult and stall_mult are 1.0 there, and each step away from it scales by these amounts. A 1 is noticeably easier to get a class through than a 5, without either being a different game.
difficulty._furniture_note: A furnished desk makes the work EASIER, not just better-marked. room_score used to feed the grade and nothing else, so a bookshelf was worth points and changed nothing you could watch. It now takes the edge off difficulty for whoever sits near it -- which is what the player expects a well-equipped desk to do.

specialism._note: The subject you trained in. Yours is a step easier to get a class through and pays better; everything else is a step harder. A lean, not a cage -- you can teach anything, and sometimes you will have to, because a class that only ever sees one subject learns one subject.

assignments._note: The paper you set. A hand is drawn at the podium and you pick one, so setting work is a decision instead of a formality. RARITY pays -- coins and the experience the children get -- and DIFFICULTY is how long the paper takes. They are rolled separately and then correlated, so a Legendary is usually demanding: the question is whether this class, on this day, can actually finish it. Work you never collect counts for half.
assignments._colour_note: Grey, green, blue, violet, gold -- the ladder every looter has trained players to read without a legend. The names are yours; the order of the colours is the one people already know.
assignments._grade_note: Rarity deliberately pays COINS and XP, never grade. The three-row balance contract is measured from work completion, and a multiplier on the lesson term would move the pillar by luck rather than by play.
assignments._hand_size_note: How many cards are drawn, rolled fresh each morning between hand_size_min and hand_size_max inclusive -- a real shuffle, not always the same count. This is the hook for a later teacher LUCK skill (more, and eventually better, options for a teacher who has earned it) -- do not hardcode a count anywhere else when that lands, read it from here.

autopilot._note: Walks you to whoever needs you next, and back to the front when nobody does. It moves your feet and NEVER presses your buttons -- the judgement of what to do at the desk stays yours, and so does the decision to stop teaching in order to go. It exists because crossing a room you can already see is not the interesting part of this game.

aide._note: A teacher's aide, hired in the staff room and paid every day. They walk the room COLLECTING FINISHED WORK -- the chore -- and they never help, settle or mark. That line is deliberate: collecting is legwork, and helping is a judgement about a particular child. Hiring somebody to do the judgement would be hiring somebody to play the game.
aide._cost_note: The wage is per DAY, so an aide is a standing decision rather than a purchase you make once and forget. In a bad term they are the thing you let go.

janitor._note: Same shape as the aide, one door over: hired in the staff room, paid every day, and they clean the room's own daily mess (mess.gd) FOR you -- one piece per interval, any time of day, not lesson-gated like the aide, because mess isn't either. Same legwork/judgement line: there is no judgement in a spill, so there is nothing here hiring somebody out of.

staff_levels._note: Both the aide and the janitor can be trained up once hired -- E on their row again spends coins to raise their level, which shortens their own interval (collect_seconds / clean_seconds). Same rising-cost-per-level shape as buying a bigger room. Capped at max_level so a levelled aide is faster, never instant.

school._note: Rooms you do not stand in. A delegated room is RESOLVED BY RUNNING THE LESSON with a hired teacher's policy driving it -- the same work, stall, disruption and grade models the player is subject to. A formula would have been far easier and every number it produced would have been a lie the player could not have produced by playing.
school._furniture_note: A delegated room's furniture is bought as a LEVEL rather than placed tile by tile. Placing furniture is a spatial puzzle about range, and the puzzle is only interesting in a room you can see. Buying the outcome is honest about that.

reputation._note: What the school is thought of, 0..100. It is the ONLY thing a badly run room costs you. The simulator showed rooms are straightforwardly profitable -- each one earns more than its wages -- so without this, 'open another room' has an obvious yes and staffing it properly is optional. Reputation is what makes a room you cannot run a liability rather than free money.
reputation._gate_note: It GATES rather than pays: how many rooms you may open, and how good the applicants are. A gate is a better shape than a bonus here -- a bonus would just be more money in a game that already has enough.
